```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Quarto applies `_brand.yml` to its HTML formats on its own. brandkit adds the
"drift" look on top, a setup call that brands your plots, and templates for
three HTML outputs: a report, a slide deck and a dashboard. (PDFs and posters
have their own article: `vignette("pdf-and-posters")`.) Quarto 1.8 or later is
required.

## The scaffolds

```{r}
library(brandkit)

create_brand_quarto_html(path = "my-project")       # report.qmd
create_brand_quarto_slides(path = "my-project")     # slides.qmd, revealjs
create_brand_quarto_dashboard(path = "my-project")  # dashboard.qmd, Shiny runtime
```

| Function | Copies |
|---|---|
| `create_brand_quarto_html()` | `_brand.yml`, `drift.scss`, `_ornaments.html`, `report.qmd`, fonts, logo |
| `create_brand_quarto_slides()` | `_brand.yml`, `drift.scss`, `_ornaments.html`, `slides.qmd`, fonts, logo |
| `create_brand_quarto_dashboard()` | `_brand.yml`, `drift.scss`, `_ornaments.html`, `dashboard.qmd`, fonts, logo |

Each function is standalone and copies one example `.qmd`, so you can run
several in the same directory: they share `_brand.yml`, the fonts and the logo
without overwriting each other. The directory is created if it doesn't exist.
Nothing is overwritten unless you pass `overwrite = TRUE`, except a
`_brand.yml` in the wrong dialect, which is converted (see
`vignette("getting-started")`).

The files that make the look:

- **`drift.scss`**: the stylesheet, built from the brand's own Sass variables
  and compiled once per colour mode. It is sectioned into shared rules (tables),
  document rules (masthead, headings, code, footer), slide rules and dashboard
  rules (navbar, cards, sidebar), and you can edit it.
- **`_ornaments.html`**: the two corner ornaments, included after the page
  body. They are filled with the page's CSS colour variables rather than hex
  values, so they follow the brand and the dark-mode toggle and never go stale.

All three templates use R's built-in `airquality` data.

## HTML reports

```yaml
---
title: "My Report"
subtitle: "A branded HTML report"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  html:
    title-block-style: none   # the .brand-masthead div supplies the title block
    theme:
      light: [brand, drift.scss]
      dark: [brand, drift.scss]
    include-after-body: _ornaments.html
---
```

```{r}
# In the document's setup chunk (`#| include: false`)
library(brandkit)
brand_quarto_setup(adaptive = TRUE)
```

The nested `light:` / `dark:` form of `theme:` is what gives readers a working
light/dark toggle: Quarto compiles one Bootstrap stylesheet per mode and the
toggle swaps them. The flat `theme: [brand, drift.scss]` form still shows a
toggle, but only the syntax highlighting switches, so keep the nested form.

The report opens with a `.brand-masthead` div (the logo, the title in the
brand's primary colour, the subtitle, a short bar in the secondary colour above
the author and date) and ends with a `.brand-footer` div. Both pull their text
from the YAML header with `{{< meta ... >}}` and are plain divs, meant to be
edited.

### Plots that follow the toggle

Plots are normally static images, so they can't follow a light/dark toggle.
`brand_quarto_setup(adaptive = TRUE)` gets round that by drawing every figure
twice, once per mode, and showing whichever matches the page. Your chunks don't
change: after each chunk that drew figures, brandkit runs its code again in dark
mode into twin files (`<label>-dark-<n>.png`), and a small script swaps the
images when the toggle flips. `brand_plotly()` writes a light and a dark widget
and a stylesheet shows the matching one. The dark version gets the dark text
colours *and* the brand's dark palette.

The costs: every plot chunk runs twice; the dark files must stay beside the page
(so `embed-resources: true` isn't supported); and a `brand_plotly()` result is a
pair of widgets that can't be piped into further plotly calls. Leave `adaptive`
off, or pass `mode =`, for a document with a single mode.

## Slides

```yaml
---
title: "My Slides"
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: [brand, drift.scss]
    include-after-body: _ornaments.html
    logo: medium
    slide-number: true
    footer: "{{< meta title >}}"
---
```

The title slide is plain type with no panel; content slides carry headings in
the primary colour; every slide has the pair of corner ornaments behind it.

Revealjs defines none of Bootstrap's colour variables, so the Slides section of
`drift.scss` defines the three the ornaments use from the brand colours of the
deck's mode, and it moves the page background onto `<html>` (reveal paints its
viewport opaque, which would hide the ornaments).

For a dark deck add `brand-mode: dark` to the YAML and call
`brand_quarto_setup("dark")`. For plotly in slides always pass fixed
dimensions: `brand_plotly(p, width = 1000, height = 600)`. Slides have no
toggle, so there is no adaptive mode for them.

## Dashboards

`create_brand_quarto_dashboard()` scaffolds a small Shiny-backed dashboard of
`airquality`: month and temperature filters in the sidebar, a row of value
boxes, two charts (one an interactive `brand_plotly()` widget) and a table.

```{r}
# In the setup chunk (`#| context: setup`)
library(brandkit)
brand_quarto_setup(shiny = TRUE)
```

Dark mode is on by default: the document declares a theme per mode, which puts
the toggle in the navbar. Plots are drawn live by Shiny, so, unlike the static
report, they follow the toggle. `brand_quarto_setup(shiny = TRUE)` is the one
line that arranges it: it switches on thematic, which gives each `renderPlot()`
the colours, font and background of its card and redraws it when the mode
changes, including the discrete palette. The plotly chart follows too, with no
`mode` argument, because inside a Shiny render `brand_plotly()` reads the
background of its card.

Because the document declares `server: shiny` it is served, not rendered:

```{r}
# in a terminal
# quarto serve dashboard.qmd
```

Add `# Page` headings for more pages; the tab strip appears once there are two.
The sample needs the `plotly` package.

## The logo in a document

```markdown
::: {.brand-logo-container}
{{< brand logo medium >}}
:::
```

The `.brand-logo-container` class limits the logo to `max-height: 48px`.
